opus-5.5.text:
Well, first I'd push back a little on the framing, because I've never been very comfortable with the term "AI" as it's used now. It suggests we've built some kind of autonomous mind, and what we've actually built is a remarkable artifact: an enormous statistical summary of what lots of humans have written, said, and done. That's a real achievement, and I don't want to diminish it. But it's important to be clear about what it is.

The limits come from that. These systems are very good at reproducing patterns that are well represented in the data. They're much weaker when it comes to genuine uncertainty: knowing what they don't know, and conveying calibrated uncertainty to someone who has to make a decision. If I'm a doctor or an engineer, I don't just want a fluent answer. I want to know how confident to be, what the evidence is, and what happens if it's wrong. That's a statistical and decision-theoretic problem, and you don't solve it just by scaling up.

The second limit, which I care about a lot, is that intelligence in the real world isn't located in a single box. It's collective. It lives in markets, in institutions, in the way people share information and coordinate under scarcity and conflicting incentives. Training one giant model on all the data and putting it in the middle of everything misses that. It ignores where the data came from, who gets value from it, and whether the people who generated it have any stake in the outcome.

So when I think about the next phase, I don't think in terms of making the model smarter in isolation. I think about systems: how learning algorithms interact with people and with each other, how you design the incentives, how you get provenance and accountability, how you handle the fact that the world isn't stationary and people respond strategically to what the system does. That combines machine learning with economics and statistics, and frankly, it's an engineering discipline we haven't really built yet. That's where I see both the limits and the opportunity.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I'm not sure "AI" is the right frame for what these systems are. What we've built are very large-scale pattern recognition and prediction engines, and they're remarkable at that. If you give them a huge corpus of human text, they'll find structure in it that we didn't know how to write down by hand. That's a genuine engineering achievement. But I've always been uncomfortable with the leap from "this system produces fluent outputs" to "this system understands" or "this system is intelligent." Those are different claims, and the gap between them is exactly where the limits show up.

Let me try to be concrete about where I see those limits.

The first is about where the data comes from and what it actually captures. These systems are trained on the record of what humans have said and done, which is a kind of imitation of collective human behavior. That's very different from having a model of the world. When you ask a question and the system gives you an answer, it's not reasoning from first principles about the underlying causal structure of the problem. It's producing something that looks like what a person might say in that context. Most of the time that's fine, because most of the time the aggregate of human knowledge is pretty good. But when you move off the distribution, when you need genuine causal understanding, or when the thing you care about is rare or novel or counterfactual, the system has no grounding to fall back on. It'll produce something plausible-sounding, and the plausibility is the dangerous part.

The second limit is uncertainty. I've spent a lot of my career on this, and I think it's underappreciated. A system that's going to be used in the real world, in medicine, in finance, in logistics, needs to know what it doesn't know. It needs to be able to say "I'm confident here" and "I'm not confident here" in a way that's calibrated and that a decision-maker can act on. Scaling up data doesn't give you that for free. In fact, the way these models are trained, they're pushed toward confident outputs because that's what the training objective rewards. So you get systems that are fluent and assertive and sometimes wrong, and there's no principled error bar attached. That's a problem of statistics, not a problem that goes away with more data.

The third limit is the one I think is most important and most neglected, which is that intelligence doesn't live inside one head. Real intelligence, the kind we actually rely on as a civilization, is collective. It's markets, it's institutions, it's scientific communities, it's the fact that I know something, you know something else, and we have mechanisms for pooling that and making decisions under uncertainty with competing incentives. The current paradigm is very much "build one giant brain in a box and ask it questions." That's a cultural inheritance from a certain strand of AI research going back decades, this idea that the goal is to replicate a human. I think that's the wrong goal. The interesting engineering problems are about systems that connect many people, many sources of data, many agents with their own objectives, and help them coordinate. Economics has been thinking about this for a couple of centuries. There's a lot there that the machine learning community has mostly ignored.

And then there's a fourth thing, which is more sociological than technical. When you train on enormous amounts of data scraped from everywhere, you've got an attribution problem and an incentive problem. Whose data was that? Who gets credit, who gets paid, who's responsible when something goes wrong? Those aren't afterthoughts. If you want these systems to be sustainable, if you want people to keep contributing the data and the feedback that makes them work, you need an economic structure around them, not just a technical one. The current approach largely sidesteps that, and I think it'll come back to bite us.

So to summarize, I'd say the limits aren't primarily about scale. More data and more compute will keep giving you better pattern matchers. The limits are about what pattern matching fundamentally isn't. It isn't causal reasoning, it isn't calibrated uncertainty, it isn't collective decision-making, and it isn't an economic system with aligned incentives. Those are the hard problems, and I'd rather we spent our energy there than on the question of whether the box in the corner is "truly intelligent."

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the first thing to separate is having a lot of data from having the right information to make a decision. You can train a system on enormous amounts of historical data, and it may become very good at predicting things under conditions similar to those it has seen. But that doesn’t automatically tell you what will happen when you intervene, when the environment changes, or when people adapt to the system.

Think about a recommendation system. It isn’t just observing people’s preferences; it’s influencing them. And if you have many such systems operating simultaneously, their decisions affect one another. Now you’re dealing with feedback, incentives, and competition. Those aren’t problems that disappear simply because you collect more data.

So I wouldn’t frame the limit as a single ceiling on intelligence. I’d ask: What is the system trying to accomplish? Whose interests does it serve? How does it represent uncertainty, and what happens when it makes a mistake? Learning from data is a powerful component, but building systems that make reliable decisions in the world requires a much broader architecture.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one limit is the assumption that more data will somehow turn prediction into understanding, or turn understanding into good decisions. Those are different problems. A system can be very good at finding patterns in historical data and still have difficulty when you intervene in the world, when circumstances change, or when its own decisions change the data it subsequently sees.

Think about a recommendation system. It isn’t simply predicting what someone wants. By choosing what to show them, it influences what they encounter and what they may want next. And when millions of people and businesses interact through such systems, you have questions about incentives, allocation, and feedback. Accuracy on a fixed dataset doesn’t tell you whether that whole system works well.

So I wouldn’t frame the issue solely as, ‘How intelligent can we make this model?’ I’d ask, ‘How do we build a system that makes useful decisions, represents uncertainty, and coordinates with people?’ Large amounts of data can help enormously. But they don’t, by themselves, specify the objectives or resolve the conflicts among the people affected.
